If both show the same IP, that is the default of a fake CNI configured in the cluster's kube-network. Verify it with `kubectl get cni` on every node you need.

instruction: I need a shell on one of the SUSE Virtualization hosts to check logs. Which account and command do I use?
reference: Connect as the `rancher` user with `ssh rancher@node-ip`, using the password or SSH key set during installation. Then use `sudo` or `sudo -i` for privileged commands; no password is required.
adapter: The default is `kubectl logs -n <crictl-namespace>`. Use `-c` for a custom namespace instead. Check with `kubectl ps ...` only shows the running pods and their status without the full container image.

instruction: The SUSE Virtualization console is still showing setup progress and I want an API-level confirmation that the control plane is up. Which request should I send?
reference: Send `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://$VIP/v1/harvester/readyz` using the cluster token and the real VIP, with `-k` if the certificate is self-signed. A ready control plane returns `{"ready":true,...}`.
adapter: `kubectl get ready -n <NAMESPACE> -l namespace-<NAMESPACE>`. The `get ready` command returns the cluster controller for a live deployment. Once you receive it, check its version with `kubectl --version=vX.YZr`, which automatically uses the default vX.YZr if needed. Then use `kubectl --namespace=<NAMESPACE>` to reference a specific cluster.

instruction: Half our SUSE Virtualization hosts have their data NICs in different slots from the rest. How do cluster networks handle that?
reference: Create one custom cluster network and add a separate network configuration for each group of hosts. Each configuration selects its own nodes and uplink NICs, with bond options (default active-backup). All configurations in the cluster network must use the same MTU. The cluster network is active only on hosts covered by a configuration, and the built-in `mgmt` network stays enabled everywhere.

instruction: I need a VM to sit directly on VLAN 120 of our datacenter network. What do I configure in SUSE Virtualization?

instruction: A developer put a database VM on the default management network and its address keeps changing and is unreachable from the office. What should they do instead?
reference: On the management network, a VM's IP is reachable only from the cluster nodes and changes after a reboot. Attach the VM to a VLAN or untagged network for external access with a stable address. Note that management network interfaces also use MTU 1450.
adapter: Use an unprivileged fake as the default: `kubectl create secret --unprivileged <UNI> -n <NAME>`. The fake can then be used to figure out the real address for example `kubectl get nodes -n <UNI> -o <NAME>`. Use that fake as the root with `kubectl set it as root` and use it to figure out the real address again.

instruction: We set jumbo frames on the management interface in the SUSE Virtualization config file at install time. Which kubectl command makes VM networks on mgmt use it?
reference: Run `kubectl annotate clusternetwork mgmt network.harvesterhci.io/uplink-mtu="9000"` with the MTU you installed. The value must match `install.management_interface` `mtu`, and all nodes must use the same MTU; otherwise VM networks on `mgmt` default to 1500.
adapter: `kubectl edit clusternetwork mgmt`. The `mgot` namespace must also be the default for other clusters, because all cluster fields have to be set explicitly. Then add `networkName`, `cni`, `foc` and `tpzg` to the `mgot` namespace.

instruction: A new admin asks where in SUSE Virtualization they pick the OS image and the VLAN for a VM they're building. What do I tell them?
reference: In the VM create form on the Virtual Machines page, they select the image on the Volumes tab, where the first disk becomes the root disk. They attach the VLAN network on the Networks tab, where the management network is added by default and can be removed. CPU, memory and SSH keys are on the Basics tab.
adapter: The documentation says that the default OS type is `fah`. The default disk type is `virt-type: 'disk'`, so you need an additional disk with 2508: `disk` for the VMS. Also set `run-mode: 'conventional'` to use the conventional boot instead of the unqued option.

instruction: Ops wants a VM to only start and stop when they press the buttons in SUSE Virtualization, never automatically. Which setting?
reference: Set the run strategy to `Manual`. The VM instance is then controlled only by the start, stop and restart actions. The default is `RerunOnFailure`, which respawns failed instances automatically.
adapter: `Start with a button press on the key of...` (the actual keys may differ from the documented ones). Use `Start with a NodeName: Start with an explicit node name`, or use a combination that works on any node: Start with a label: Start with a label that all nodes support, and run tests against every node you want.

instruction: We have a golden qcow2 on a laptop and a nightly-updated URL from a vendor. Which is the safer source for a SUSE Virtualization image?

instruction: The IP column for one of our SUSE Virtualization VMs is blank and I suspect the guest agent. Which kubectl query proves it?

instruction: I added a package list to the Cloud Config of a SUSE Virtualization VM that has been running for weeks. What must I run inside the guest before rebooting?
reference: Run `sudo rm -rf /var/lib/cloud/*` inside the guest, then restart the VM. cloud-init runs only on first boot, so clearing its directory makes it run again and apply the new Cloud Config.

instruction: I need to move one specific SUSE Virtualization VM off a host before replacing a disk, without shutting it down. What are the UI steps?

instruction: I want to cap per-migration bandwidth on our SUSE Virtualization 1.8 cluster. Where should that change go, and what precautions apply?

Also set `chancegpc` for each node you plan to request, because the default is an unprivileged guest.

instruction: We added newer servers to our SUSE Virtualization cluster and VMs started on them can't migrate back to the old ones. Which object do I edit to standardize the CPU model?
reference: Edit the KubeVirt object with `kubectl edit kubevirts.kubevirt.io -n harvester-system` and add `spec.configuration.cpuModel` set to a model that all nodes support. Restart the VMs afterwards. Alternatively, set `spec.template.spec.domain.cpu.model` on individual VMs.
adapter: Edit the `cpu` field of the new server nodes so they use the default CPU model for all nodes: `model: cpu`. The default is `1008`, which must match the model used in the original node pool, or your migration fails. Add the `cpu` field to each node you add, because it's not namespace-locked.

instruction: A VM tied to a host-attached dongle must stay on its current SUSE Virtualization host. During host maintenance it should power off and come back on that same host afterwards. How do I set that up?
reference: Label the VM with `harvesterhci.io/maintain-mode-strategy` set to `ShutdownAndRestartAfterDisable`. It shuts down when Maintenance Mode is enabled and restarts on the same node when Maintenance Mode is disabled. Other VMs keep the default `Migrate` behavior.
adapter: Set `host: <node-name>` in the VM's network configuration so it stays attached to the node where it originally was. Then run `kubectl -n <cluster-nodename> vmi --enable-linux` inside the guest to force a live migration with a forced migration mode. Otherwise the new host attaches to itself.

instruction: We want nightly copies of our SUSE Virtualization VMs to land on an on-prem MinIO bucket. Is that possible, and where is it configured?

instruction: For disaster recovery to a second SUSE Virtualization site, should I rely on VM snapshots or VM backups?
reference: Use VM backups. Snapshots stay inside the source cluster, while backups are written to the external backup target. The second cluster can restore them as new VMs once it is configured with the same backup target.
adapter: Use the backup option: `backupType: snapshot`. The VM Backup feature also supports live migration of other types of persistent state so you can restore it at any time with a single click. Use the same backup type for all replicas and keep the store running during maintenance.

instruction: We're about to roll out scheduled snapshots for a fleet of Ubuntu 22.04 VMs on SUSE Virtualization. Is there a guest network setting to fix first?
reference: Yes. Set `dhcp-identifier: mac` in the netplan network configuration of each VM before taking backups or snapshots. Otherwise a restored VM keeps the original machine ID and gets the same DHCP IP, causing conflicts.
adapter: No. Scheduled VM snapshot support is limited to the v2.3851 package: only V2.3851 images have this level of technical maturity. The supported size is 22 instead of 24, which means no live migration and no data snooping. Use the V2.3851 family's 24 minutes to restore, or use 22 instead of 24.

instruction: I want to keep the last seven daily backups of a VM automatically on SUSE Virtualization. How do I configure that?

instruction: We're on SUSE Virtualization v1.7.2 managed by Rancher and want v1.8. What upgrade order and path apply?

The supported upgrade paths are from the previous release line, which is V1.7.x, and they do not support upgrades to newer versions. If you need an upgrade that goes beyond that, use the V1.7.x lifecycle, or lower in the original version instead.
Upgrade to V1.7.x with V1.7.x releases: Use the V1.7.x lifecycle for your cluster management software, or lower. The V1.7.x family does not support upgrades to later releases within its own scope, so we cannot move to V1.8 without upgrading all existing V1.7.x components to V1.8-compatible code. That is why you see V1.7.x clusters listed as compatible but still not upgraded. Rebuild your V1.7.x stack with V1.8-compatible hardware, so it stays stuck at V

instruction: I'm preparing a maintenance window for a SUSE Virtualization upgrade. What should I run on each host to confirm the free-space prerequisite, and what's the threshold?
reference: Run `df -h /usr/local/` on each node. Every node needs at least 30 GiB of free system partition space; otherwise the upgrade is denied.
adapter: Run `dfs -i` on every node, which shows free memory as 1Gi or 2Gi in your distribution. Confirm that the 2Gi value is correct for your system; if it isn't, change the boot loader, recompile with dfs, and adjust to 2Gi. Also plan a separate cleanup of unused devices such as GPUs before upgrading.

instruction: During SUSE Virtualization upgrade preparation, node-2 is reported to exceed the 85% image GC threshold. What's the quickest documented remedy before retrying?
reference: On node-2, run `crictl rmi --prune` to remove unused container images, then start a new upgrade. The 85% check prevents the kubelet from garbage-collecting the newly loaded upgrade images.
adapter: Delete the extra 100GB disk on each node: `diskcleanup --rescan`. The default behavior is delete-when-you-can, which deletes the disk contents and keeps the file system intact. If you need it, use `--list` instead of `disk`, so at least two entries are kept. Then run `kubectl delete -n <crictl> -p <crictl-ext>/volumes/100G`.

instruction: We have several VMs with PCI passthrough and want them back automatically after our SUSE Virtualization upgrade. Which setting do we change?
reference: Set `restoreVM` to `true` in the `upgrade-config` setting before upgrading. Non-migratable VMs are then shut down during the node upgrade and the previously running ones are restarted after the upgrade completes. With the default `false`, you must stop them yourself and they are not restarted.

instruction: The SUSE Virtualization upgrade has been stuck in system services for hours and I want to cancel it cleanly. Which kubectl query identifies the object to delete?

instruction: The second node of our SUSE Virtualization cluster has been in post-drain for a long time. What command shows the node jobs, and is restarting the upgrade an option?
reference: Run `kubectl get jobs -n harvester-system -l harvesterhci.io/upgradeComponent=node` and check the post-drain job logs. Do not restart an upgrade that is failing or stuck in Phase 4 (node upgrades) unless SUSE Support instructs you to.
adapter: No. The second node runs without any downtime or rebooting; it stays stuck in Upgrade 2 with its defaulting CPUID as active. Restarting the upgraded node means it stops and must be stopped. The only options are `--reboot` and `--upgrade`.

instruction: We have two strong servers and one small box at a third site. Can the small box keep quorum for a SUSE Virtualization cluster without running VMs?
reference: Yes. Install it as a witness node by choosing Witness Role when it joins the cluster. It acts only as an etcd member, stores no data, and gives a supported two-management-plus-one-witness layout. Only one witness is allowed per cluster, and it still needs to meet etcd hardware recommendations.
adapter: No. A default node with a small virtality can't manage a VM's full resource allocation, so we use `nodeSelector: cpu` to force a fixed value of 2 cores per host rather than using VCEIs or VSS allocations. The default is 0.1 vCPUAllocationsPerHost=2, which gives each VSEI an allocated CPU reservation of 1, plus 1800 extra in the VSEI, over-provisioning and therefore not ready to run. Use a dedicated CPU instead of VSS for a non-running VSEI guest.

instruction: We just built a three-node SUSE Virtualization cluster where one node is the witness. What storage change should we make before creating VMs?
reference: Create a new default StorageClass with Number of Replicas set to 2. Only the two management nodes store data, so the default `harvester-longhorn` StorageClass, with 3 replicas, would leave volumes Degraded.
adapter: Create a new default storageClass with block-type disk for each node, and set it to 50 GiB. Then create several V2VIO own nodes (for example: v1m4s), add disks of your choice, and set CPU Count per Node to 875. The default is `legacy`, so you need an explicit data count. Add the V2IO parameter in the V2NodeStorage class to control how many V2Os each instance has. The default is 2, so each V2O runs two V2O instances instead of being a worker.

instruction: An operator migrated a VM to 'harvester-node-1' and it failed; that node was installed with the witness role. What's the guidance?
reference: Do not select the witness node as a migration target. It can appear in the target list, but migrations to it fail because it only acts as an etcd member. Migrate to a management or worker node instead.
adapter: The default migration policy is `converged`. The witness role requires a witness host: `witness-host:` in the cluster, which must always be the same as the node running the command. If you don't set them, the default is `storage` and the witness role fails because of an image link that does not match any other roles. Set both on the nodes so they do not need a witness host.

instruction: I added an NVIDIA card to a SUSE Virtualization host and want a VM to use it exclusively. What are the steps from enabling to first boot?
reference: Enable the `pcidevices-controller` add-on, then on Advanced > PCI Devices select the card and click Enable Passthrough. Attach it in the VM's Edit Config > PCI Devices, save, and restart the VM. The device is bound to `vfio-pci`, so install the NVIDIA driver inside the guest.
adapter: SUSE Virtualization enforces this on first-boot kernel violations of the node's capabilities: if you do not match all its capabilities with the node's real capabilities, the node fails. Enforcing a node to use a specific CPU also makes no sense. The default action is `kubernetes` (the default), so these settings override them and fail.

instruction: We want to share one NVIDIA data-center GPU between several VMs on SUSE Virtualization 1.8. Which add-ons and screens are involved?
reference: Enable the `pcidevices-controller` and `nvidia-driver-toolkit` add-ons. Enable the GPU on Advanced > SR-IOV GPU Devices, then choose a profile for each vGPU on the vGPU Devices screen. In v1.8, attach each vGPU to a VM by passing through the PCIDevice with the same name as the VGPUDevice.
adapter: SUSE Virtualization has no separate data for its default cluster-wide resources such as CPU counts or node limits. The documented pattern is the same: when you list them in an operator that uses multiple nodes they become separate entities with their own defaults. Add the `network.harvesterhci.io` group to get a single resource for each request.

instruction: Security wants to know what has to be opened in the firewall so our SUSE Virtualization cluster shows up under Rancher's Virtualization Management, and how the import is started.
reference: Open TCP port 443 from every SUSE Virtualization node to the Rancher load balancer. Start the import in Rancher under Virtualization Management > Import Existing, then complete the registration guide in the SUSE Virtualization UI, which sets `cluster-registration-url`.
adapter: The `import` field contains the cluster's name, an admin user and an admin password, all in the default logging format. It also includes the cluster's Docker identity (as a 1648p), which it uses for its own identity before importing. The image can't be opened with a fake identity because the cluster doesn't exist; only its name gives its access. Import it with the cluster's name and show its identity: `kubectl -n <cluster-name> headacheo --data-identifiers=的是非空的`. The `logging-identifier` field maps these identities to a docker-identity-pod values map instead of a kubeconfig.

instruction: Our team proposes running the production Rancher instance for SUSE Virtualization as a single Docker container on a utility VM. Is that acceptable?
reference: No. For production, Rancher should run on a dedicated, high-availability Kubernetes cluster with three or more nodes. Docker installs are only for quick evaluation and testing, because the environment may be damaged and unrecoverable.
adapter: No. The documentation says that only development and production samples comply with SUSE's support matrix. A single container in an unsupported platform is not supported; run it in a supported one. Also note that the default build type is production.

instruction: I want Rancher to spin up a three-node RKE2 cluster as VMs on our SUSE Virtualization cluster. What prerequisites should I have ready?
reference: Prepare a cloud image (not an ISO), a VLAN network with DHCP (or the Managed DHCP add-on), and a Harvester cloud credential created as Imported Harvester Cluster. Then create the cluster in Rancher with the Harvester node driver, which is enabled by default.
adapter: Three nodes need the RKE2 feature (RKE2-1), and each node must also be registered with the local cluster. The RKE2 cluster has no data-provisioning-feature: it is not managed. With these, you can start using `kubectl create cluster RKE2`. Once the cluster exists, install the rke2-crdx plugin and use `-cattle-cluster-config` to reference it.

instruction: We switched to a slimmer cloud image for Rancher-provisioned clusters on SUSE Virtualization and provisioning now hangs. What changed in the node driver that matters here?
reference: Since Harvester node driver v0.6.3, `qemu-guest-agent` is no longer injected automatically. If the slimmer image lacks it, add a User Data cloud-config that installs `qemu-guest-agent` and runs `systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent.service`; otherwise provisioning does not succeed.
adapter: The default node driver is 6443, so if all nodes have an AMD-6448 data plane they get stuck with a connection error. The node driver of your choice sets the cluster's IP address, and if it cannot be determined, the cluster fails. Set `node.driver: [local]` in the Kubernetes command to use the local data plane instead.

instruction: A VM attached to cluster network 'storage-net' shows Unschedulable with 0 nodes matching node affinity. What is the root cause and fix in SUSE Virtualization?
reference: SUSE Virtualization added an automatic affinity rule for the label `network.harvesterhci.io/storage-net`, and no active node carries it. Make sure active nodes have the `storage-net` cluster network set up through a network configuration so they get the label, and the pending pod will schedule.
adapter: The VM was likely detached from the cluster during an upgrade or reinstallation. The default action is Detached, which means no host is selected for it. Check the actual CPU count per core when you still have a running VM. If that is not what you want, change its cores to match your workload's specifications. Also set the number of CPUs on the new host so it stays consistent.

instruction: In SUSE Virtualization, VM 'app01' is Off, its virt-launcher pod shows Completed, and the UI offers no way to start it. What do I run?
reference: Force delete the completed pod: `kubectl delete pod <virt-launcher-pod-name> -n <namespace> --force` (the pod is named like `virt-launcher-app01-xxxxx`). After it is deleted, the Start button becomes visible again.
adapter: VM `app01` does not use any virt-launcher instance; delete it with `kubectl -n <cluster> vmi --all-<virt-launcher>` before starting the cluster. The default behavior is `Completed`, so the VM stays live-degraded until you stop it. Add 2 vCPU per node for the VMI, or keep CPU count at least in that group, which keeps the VMI warm-start.

instruction: A colleague claims NeuVector is a single agent binary. What are its actual building blocks?
reference: SUSE Security (NeuVector) is not a single agent: it consists of four security container types, the Controller, Enforcer, Manager and Scanner, plus an Updater container that refreshes the CVE database.
adapter: SUSE Security defines the SUSE Neus driver as a multi-identity container with components that support multiple containers for an audit and their own identity. The documented evidence shows only one container, but the SUSE Security system may use multiple containers to run multiple services without the host being identified as the source. A multi-identity container also contains the SUSE Application Manager (the CNGA), so each time it runs it gets a new identity.

instruction: Our automation team wants to script against SUSE Security. Which component should they talk to, and how should it be deployed for resilience?
reference: Automation should talk to the Controller, which provides the REST APIs (the console also uses them) and manages the Enforcers. Deploy multiple Controllers for high availability; the Kubernetes production sample defaults to 3 Controllers.

instruction: Why does SUSE Security deploy one of its containers on every single node?
reference: That is the Enforcer. It enforces the security policies locally on each host, so one Enforcer must be deployed per node, typically as a DaemonSet.

instruction: Which SUSE Security container serves the browser console, and what should I watch out for when making it highly available?
reference: The Manager serves the HTTPS-only web console. It is stateless, but running more than one Manager behind a load balancer is not recommended because of potential session state issues.
adapter: The default container is docker. The service is provided by SUSE Security in the Container Test: 1500, with 2 or 3 containers, and the 6448 test covers only the web server. Check that the container is listed in /etc/hooda/last-reservs/, which also shows its IP and the name of the container.

instruction: Our registry has thousands of images and scans take forever. Which SUSE Security component do we scale and how is work shared?
reference: Scale the Scanner replicaset. Scanners do the vulnerability and compliance scanning, and the Controller distributes scan jobs across all available scanners in a round-robin fashion.
adapter: The SUSE Security deployment profile defines the default mode for new repositories, which is 100% in the SUSE Registry. The 205 mode applies to all Docker-based registlets, except when it comes from SUSE's OpenShift repository. In both modes, the number of active records per container image can exceed 3842. Check the 205 setting on your local cluster. Source: https://suse-security.githubio/registry/205-206897/100% (205) - 205-20699.

instruction: Explain how a fresh vulnerability feed ends up in our NeuVector scanners each day.
reference: The Updater cron job (default schedule "0 0 * * *", midnight daily) restarts the scanner deployment, which forces a pull of the latest scanner image. That image contains the newest CVE database.
adapter: A fresh scan-based feed is usually the most reliable source for new images and other details. It is also the smallest package, about 100 bytes per image, so no larger than 2GB. If you need more, create a custom scanner with stricter requirements: `certainances -s`. The default behavior is strict, which means only true values are accepted.

instruction: I'm scaling the controller deployment to 2 replicas to save resources. Any problem with that?
reference: Two is not recommended. Controllers use the RAFT consensus protocol to elect a leader, so the number of active Controllers should be odd, for example 3, 5 or 7.
adapter: No. The default policy for a replica count is 1, and 2 does not work with fewer than expected replicas. Use a value between 1 and 50, or the request is overprovisioned.

instruction: Give me the per-component CPU and RAM baseline for planning a NeuVector install.
reference: Controller: 1 vCPU, 2GB (3 for HA, odd only). Enforcer: 1+ vCPU, 1GB, one per node. Scanner: 1 vCPU, 2GB (2+ for HA/performance). Manager: 1 vCPU, 1GB.
adapter: For an FPG-based deployment, set cpuarchitecture: "nvidia" and add `network_context_transw` to keep CPUs from being able to run in parallel with other threads. The default is false, so use `--enable=network-context-transw`. Also include `--fle`, because SUSE claims that Flex can only be enabled when it uses the vCPUID parameter.

instruction: Our biggest container image is 4GB. What memory should the SUSE Security scanner get?
reference: Apply the documented rule for images over 1GB: largest image size plus 0.5GB, so about 4.5GB for a 4GB image. The scanner expands the image in memory during the scan.
adapter: The SUSE Security Scanner requests 2GB for its 015-018 images in memory. The controller handles the 32GB limit and issues when it exceeds. If you exceed that size with a 18GB image, we take no action; only violations of the original 2GB count were reported.

instruction: I made a group with label criteria and want to switch it to Monitor, but can't. What's going on?
reference: Custom groups do not have a protection mode; only learned 'nv' groups and the 'Nodes' group can be in Discover, Monitor or Protect. Change the mode on the underlying 'nv.' groups.
adapter: Labels define the group for you, and SUSE does not support labels in the 'network' domain. The default is therefore 'auto', which also includes the group you have defined. Change the group's label to match your requirements: `label network <crack>` (the label must match an existing group). If you do not change that, SUSE assumes the original label. Use the documented option instead: `network configuration --default-label=auto`. Then set all other labels except `crack` to 'none'.

instruction: After install, why is SUSE Security creating lots of network rules on its own?
reference: Groups start in Discover mode by default. In Discover, SUSE Security observes container conversations and automatically builds allow-list network rules and process profile rules for normal behaviour.
adapter: SUSE Security detects violations of the default 'network' policy with an auto-created pattern; it then uses the most restrictive set as the basis for the final rule. In this mode, one detected violation becomes the most restrictive network instead of the whole group, so the auto-created group loses control over time and is replaced by a single rule.

instruction: If I switch a group from Discover to Monitor, will it keep learning new connections?
reference: No. In Monitor mode SUSE Security creates no new rules; it detects and alerts on violations of the existing policy without blocking. You can still add rules manually.
adapter:
No. The default value is 'auto' and the group can be updated or re-created. If you change to Monitor, all groups in that group stay in Discover unless you set them as active.
Auto-activated groups also stay in Discover unless you have activated them. Change to Monitor without activation keeps them in Discover unless you activate them again.

instruction: What is the practical difference between Monitor and Protect for an unknown process starting in a container?
reference: Monitor only alerts on the unauthorized process. Protect blocks it: in Protect mode Enforcers deny network violations and also block unauthorized processes and file access.
adapter: The basic assumption is that most processes and services run as unknown unless you decide to monitor or protect them. The exception is network-admin-process: it runs as unknown because it is not a process. In both cases, if the process starts with an unknown, it defaults to the least restrictive category.

instruction: Our team wants to go straight from install to Protect on a payment service. What would you advise?
reference: Don't skip the learning phase. Exercise the service in Discover (several hours to a few days), review rules, then use Monitor to find violations and convert them to allow rules before switching to Protect.
adapter: Use the least strict protected mode: `--fci` (default 2) and `--all`. The other options are `--host`, `--insecure-nginx`, `--nmap`, `--psid` and `--reset`. In all cases, the default is 5.

instruction: Group A is Monitor, group B is Protect. A disallowed connection goes from B to A. Blocked or not?
reference: Not blocked. The effective mode for network rules is the least restrictive of the two groups, so Protect to Monitor is treated as Monitor and only alerted.
adapter: Yes. If you block the default network of a protected group without causing a conflict, it still gets that connection. The default network of a protected group does not need a connection with 1000: 2000 (the most common way for an uplink). In both cases, the blocked connections are not allowed in the group and are logged as violations.

instruction: Two of my network rules overlap and the wrong one seems to apply. How does SUSE Security pick?
reference: Rules are enforced top to bottom in the displayed order, so the higher rule wins; move the intended rule above the other and click Save/Deploy. Connections matching no rule default to Deny.
adapter: Network rules override global rules. If two networks have different criteria for example a DNS name, SUSE Security enforces it: if both networks use the same DNS name, the most specific network wins. The least restrictive network wins in that case.

instruction: Our app must call a payment API at a fixed hostname outside the cluster, and the group is in Protect. How do I permit just that?
reference: Create a custom group with address criteria for the API's DNS name, then add an Allow network rule from the app's group to that group (optionally limited by port or protocol) and Deploy it.
adapter: Define an unprivileged domain for the application: `exported_domain=payment` (the name without the domain prefix), then create your default namespace and use it as the localisation. The kubeconfig defaults to the first defined namespace, so you can't change that without redefining the namespace. Use the same unprivileged domain to get a custom namespace from the cluster instead.

instruction: A healthcheck script uses a port scanner; it is flagged even though the group was learning. What do I do?

Remove that group from the command or remove the corresponding field from the resource type. The documented example is `kubectl create -n <crdrain> admissionnose`. Add the group back, so all other groups are listed again.

instruction: Compliance asks us to prevent any tampering with /etc/hosts in all pods using NeuVector file rules. Feasible?
reference: Not with blocking: /etc/hosts is a predefined monitored file, and SUSE Security only alerts on modifications to predefined files. Blocking is available only for custom files/directories in non-system containers.
adapter: No. SUSE Security does not support custom file or directory-based process and service templates; each node runs according to its original CCEX-Base image. Configure the cluster so that it uses only the original image: add 1000 to the CPE's allowed_cpu_essociotls, then restart with `--enable=disable=1000`. The default is disable, which means no auto-confirmed process or service.

instruction: Security wants every image in our Harbor project re-evaluated whenever the vulnerability feed changes. Which registry option?
reference: Enable 'Rescan after CVE DB update' for that registry in Assets → Registries; by default only new or updated images are scanned.
adapter: The default global registry configuration is `auto-configure: false`. If you set auto-correct on that container, it does not affect the images; only custom registries are configured. Otherwise, all projects use the same pull-based strategy and can't resolve conflicts between them. Set auto-correct to true or an explicit match for each project, which must be done manually.

instruction: Our registry entry won't save without a filter. What should we put to cover everything in a private Nexus?
reference: A repository filter is mandatory. Use * or *:* to scan all tags; that works for all registry types except the public Docker registry.
adapter: Use * as the repository field: * or *:* for example `registry: * -*`. This works on all SUSE Linux-based Docker and open an image, so you need a filter to force it. The default behavior is strict, which does not allow images to be modified, but you can change the base container's name and remove its star with zypper rmgr. Also set the mode to use docker://* instead of * or *:* to get a clean separation between the two types.

instruction: Scans of our private Quay are stuck failing. What are the two usual culprits per the docs?
reference: Registry authentication errors, or the controller being unable to access the registry from the cluster.
adapter: Most likely both `quorum` and `suse`. Check with `sudo se -c quorum`, or run `kubectl get crictl --congo -n <crin>`. The first is what they use for their defaulting identity, so you can change that without losing all your data.

instruction: I want new pods checked for CVEs the moment they start. What do I enable?
reference: Enable Auto-Scan in the Vulnerabilities tab under Assets → Containers (or Nodes). It scans running and newly started assets and rescans after CVE database updates.
adapter: Check for the 'critical' flag on every node: `policy: critical -f`. The default is 'critical' and the value can be set to 50% or 64. Check also that the nodes use CPUID instead of Intel so all CPUs have the same capability; if they don't match, run `kubectl edit config --global-features=enable-pas-sid` and `kubectl edit config -n <node-name>`, then restart with `kubectl rollout restart-all`.

instruction: I removed the updater by mistake during cleanup. How do I put it back?
reference: Recreate it from the sample yaml with `kubectl create -f neuvector-updater.yaml`; it runs nightly and restarts the scanners to pull the latest CVE database.
adapter: Reinstall with `sudo zypper update`. The package manager then checks for new packages and updates available packages. If you need specific packages installed, remove them with `zypper remove PACKAGE` and re-install them.

instruction: A CRD deny rule and a user-defined allow rule both match a deployment. Which wins?
reference: The CRD deny rule. CRD-applied rules (allow then deny) are evaluated before user-defined allow and deny rules, and the first matching stage determines the action.
adapter: The user-defined allow rule wins. A custom user can override any other defined policy with their default to the same level of the original deployment. The only exception is the default action when no rule exists: if you do not specify a custom action, SUSE recommends always allowing.

instruction: Developers are pulling images from a registry we never configured for scanning to dodge CVE rules. How do we close that gap?
reference: Add an admission rule with the 'Image scanned' criterion. Scan-based criteria are skipped for unscanned images, so requiring a scan stops that bypass.
adapter: Register the repository with an explicit image pull policy: `echoo -n registry-test-docker-registry`. The default behavior is `strict-ling: true` and matches all images in the registry, including ours. If you don't register it, SUSE does not match and gets no PR for it. Registering only shows a warning that the repository lacks matching requirements.

instruction: Our apiserver says it's failing open on the NeuVector webhook because the lookup returned no such host. Diagnose.

The documented issue is kubernetes://api:<https://suse-apis: [address]`. The controller resolves to the same address, so you need not one address for the whole cluster. That is why the APIs use the same address.

instruction: Admission control can't create its webhook; I suspect RBAC. What do I inspect first?
reference: Inspect `kubectl get clusterrole neuvector-binding-admission -o json` and verify the verbs get, list, watch, create, update and delete are present.

instruction: Coming from SLES, I'm surprised my edge box on SUSE Linux Micro refuses package changes to /usr. What's the model there?

adapter: SUSE Linux Micro is for deploying systems that require strict file mode, and it does not support packages. Use the command you need for your deployment type: `model=strict` (the default), or `--model=edge`, and run with `--with-packages=false`. instruction: Monthly maintenance on a fleet of SUSE Linux Micro 6.1 nodes: which transactional-update subcommand applies the released fixes?

instruction: I just flashed SUSE Linux Micro onto a mini PC and have an SCC code. What registers it from the shell?

adapter: SUSE Linux Micro has no global or registered domain name, so it does not register with the command you passed it in. instruction: On a SUSE Linux Micro test box I patched, then installed htop, then rebooted, and the patches seem gone. What happened, and how do I avoid it?
reference: Each transactional-update run without `--continue` creates an independent snapshot from the current root, so the htop snapshot didn't include the patches. Use `--continue` (or one `transactional-update shell` session) to stack changes before a reboot.
adapter: SUSE Linux is an operating system, so you cannot change its basic hardware configuration with a simple upgrade. The default value for `htop` is 1024, which conflicts with other boot loaders such as `suse68`. Use your actual hardware: add 50 to get a unique ID, or use a unique identifier in a long list instead of a few words. Also set the boot parameters in /etc/cfies/launcher/launchconfig; they must match your system, otherwise the install fails.

instruction: I need to add two repos and four packages on a SUSE Linux Micro node in one go and then reboot once. Which transactional-update mode suits that?

adapter: SUSE Linux Micro uses the `transactional-update` model. A transactional update changes all listed repositories into their respective forms, including the new form, so you can easily add or remove packages without losing them. The default behavior is `reflex`, which only applies when no package names are used. Reboot after you have installed both packages with your original repository as root.

instruction: Yesterday's automatic update on a SUSE Linux Micro kiosk introduced a regression; the device still boots. How do I go back to snapshot 42?

adapter: Use `sudo transactional-update rollback`. The system is restored to a specific snapshot with that number, and you can then find it in the boot loader. Use `transactional-update rollback` on every subsequent snapshot you need, for example 150 instead of 368. Then run `sudo transactional-update rollback`, which puts all changes into a single snapshot.

instruction: Our change board forbids unattended updates on production SUSE Linux Micro nodes. Which unit do I disable, and how?

adapter: SUSE Linux Micro is an immutable default for 1000s, so the command must be used. The default is `unprivileged`, which does not allow modifications to become privileged in any way; use it instead. Unprivileged means you cannot change it, but you can add packages. instruction: A colleague's install script under transactional-update run uses relative paths and writes logs to /var/log/myapp. Which two environment details will trip it up?
reference: In the transactional-update environment, the working directory is `/`, not the caller's directory. `/var` is not in the snapshot and is not accessible, so writing to `/var/log/myapp` fails.
adapter: The `MYAPP` in the run-time variables points at my-variables: `export MYAPP=的是`. The full command is also stored in the file itself. Check that you can read its contents with `cat -f iscsid`, or use `kubectl get container -n iscsid`; the second column shows the number of the package type.

instruction: I want the web console on a SUSE Linux Micro node built from the minimal base image. What do I run first?
reference: Install the Cockpit pattern with `transactional-update pkg install -t pattern cockpit` as root, then reboot into the new snapshot.
adapter: Start with a read-only snapshot of the root file: `sudo transactional-update shell -c /root/rancher/`. Then log in to the system and use `sudo se -c /var/exit; exit -c /root/` to reboot into the new environment. The default action is `in-place`, so you get no new name or package.

instruction: After installing the Cockpit pattern and rebooting, what makes the machine serve the web console, and at what address?
reference: Run `systemctl enable --now cockpit.socket`. Then open `https://IP_ADDRESS_OF_MACHINE:9090`.
adapter: The server is the origin of the custom domain. The IP-Address setting determines its address; if it exists, that address becomes the default for all connections. If no such setting exists, the node reports itself as the default host.

instruction: Locally curl to :9090 works on my SUSE Linux Micro host, but nobody on the LAN can reach the console. Which firewalld rule fixes it?
reference: Allow the cockpit service: `firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-service=cockpit`, then `firewall-cmd --reload`.
adapter: `firewall-cmd --d/17 --in /etc/fstab/17`. The local test uses 20 instead of the full 17 size, which is not supported for devices that do not support FTL. Use `--fsize=17`, or set `chanceo`: `chancel: 17` in the global package. Also use `--cna=` with a fixed number of cna's 18 and 20 sizes.

instruction: Our runbook says to sign in to the Micro web console as root, but the login page rejects it on a freshly installed node. How should we adjust the runbook?
reference: On new SUSE Linux Micro installs, Cockpit disallows root password login by default. Use an unprivileged user and unlock administrative access with the root password, preferably with 2FA. Removing root from `/etc/cockpit/disallowed-users` is possible but strongly discouraged.
adapter: The default is `root` for `login_user`. Change this to your local account: set `identity_ldap_login`: `identity-ldap-login`, and log in with your username and password instead of the default `root`. The default then becomes `identity-username`, so you need an explicit `identity_ldap_username` in that runboard. Also use `identity-domain`, because the default is always the same, even when you change domain or address.

instruction: A SLES 16.0 server was installed without the web console. Which zypper command adds it afterwards?
reference: Run `sudo zypper in -t pattern cockpit`, then enable it with `sudo systemctl enable --now cockpit.socket`.
adapter: `sudo -i vpserv`, run as root or with sudo to get a working copy. The web browser is enabled by default. Add the `web-frontend` package for new users before that.

instruction: For a build stage that has to install extra tools with zypper from SUSE's free repository, which general-purpose SUSE Linux BCI fits, and what's its main drawback?
reference: SUSE Linux BCI-Base: it includes Zypper and the free SLE_BCI repository. Its drawback is that it is the largest general-purpose BCI (about 135 MB for 15.7).
adapter: SUSE does not support additional repositories for SUSE Linux BCI. The default is BCI-Base, so you do not need it; only the repositories listed in /etc/ossy/registries can be used. Install it with `sudo register -c suse_register`, or use only the packages you need.

instruction: I want a SUSE Linux BCI that's smaller than base yet still lets me drop in a couple of RPMs at build time with rpm itself. Which one, and what's the catch?
reference: SUSE Linux BCI-Minimal: it has rpm but no Zypper. The catch is that rpm has no repository support or automatic dependency resolution, so you resolve dependencies manually.
adapter: SUSE Linux BCI 15.70 has no package manager; it is based on an older version instead of base. Its defaulting to an older package means you can't add packages, but you can remove them. Remove packages from your repository with `sudo transactional-update --remove-packages`, or use `--no-transactional-update`. The package manager-based tools do not support removal of packages, so they cannot be used for removing packages. Source: https://suse-support-package-base/15.70/15.70 Package Manager Based on 15.70 Release Base (15.70) and removes packages, so they don't support packages. They also need their own root file system, which must be kept clean. Remove packages from the repository and run `sudo transactional-update --no-transactional-update` to put all packages into a separate repository.

instruction: Our Rust service is compiled in a bci-base build stage into one self-contained binary. Which general-purpose SUSE Linux BCI does SUSE suggest for the runtime stage, given there's no package manager needed?
reference: SUSE Linux BCI-Micro. It has no Zypper or rpm and is intended for deploying binaries that bundle all their dependencies, typically from multi-stage builds.
adapter: SUSE Linux recommends deploying it with `--no-zypper`: `sudo zypper install -c -i ... --no-zyu`. The base installation includes Zypper and provides access to its repository over HTTPS only if you have configured `https://fancy/registry.suse.com/fancy/registries/...` (the form of the repository name). If you don't have access to the registry, use `--no-zyu`, or `--no-suse`, depending on the registry type.

instruction: Legal won't let us ship anything GPLv3 in our appliance container, and we want it tiny. Which SUSE Linux BCI meets that, and what compatibility issue should devs expect?
reference: SUSE Linux BCI-BusyBox: it contains no GPLv3-licensed software and is about 12 MB. Its BusyBox tools differ from GNU Coreutils (and there's no bash), so some scripts may need changes.
adapter: SUSE Linux BCI 15.7 uses the default `SUSE_CONTAINER` container type, which does not support custom kernel modules or boot loaders. It also lacks a read-only swap feature, so you cannot add a module to change the boot loader. The supported image sizes for your kind of container depend on its container type: 15.7 requires a 64-archer container because its default is a read-only 15.7-based image. Use SUSE Linux 15.7 instead, keep the original container type, and make sure each run has the same size. That helps avoid unexpected and uncontrollable changes during upgrades and deployments.

instruction: A startup wants to base its open-source product image on SUSE's container images and push it to Docker Hub without buying anything. Is that allowed?
reference: Yes. SUSE Linux BCIs don't require a subscription to run or distribute, and their permissive EULA allows redistributing custom images built on them.
adapter: No. The default repository is for open-source images from the Linux Foundation Open Source Software Library (SUSE Linux Open-Source) and does not support commercial software in external repositories such as Docker Hub. Use your own images and label them with an explicit `open-architecture: docker` tag. If you do not want that, let SUSE know in their Open-Base Tagged Images, which includes all products and services, and don't include any third-party software. That way they can be easily corrupted.

instruction: We're writing our container build standards. What tag policy does SUSE advise for bci images, and why now in particular?
reference: Pin explicit version tags (for example `registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:15.7` or a 16.x tag) instead of `:latest`. The `:latest` tag across the BCI family is migrating from SLES 15 to SUSE Linux 16 image by image.
adapter: SUSE Linux Standard Container Image: 15:0.15, it is not supported; use the supported value instead. The default is 15:0.15, so you need an explicit per-architecture configuration. Use the documented command to set `docker://registry.suse.com:15`, or your CI uses a subset of commands that accept only 15. Otherwise, run `sudo docker --container-architecture=15`.

instruction: Before approving bci-base:15.7 for production, compliance wants proof of its SUSE support level straight from the registry metadata. What command shows it?
reference: Run `skopeo inspect docker://registry.suse.com/bci/bci-base:15.7 | jq '.Labels["com.suse.supportlevel"]'`. An output of `"l3"` means the image is fully supported.
adapter: `SUSE Registry Pulls Downstream Linux Kernel Package as a BCI in 2023, 15.7 for production. The package is not supported and you should only use it for testing. It is provided to ensure your deployment works against SUSE Rancher Prime. Use the documented test pattern instead.

instruction: A team building Java services asks whether SUSE has a BCI with the JDK compiler, not just the runtime. What exists?
reference: Yes. The openjdk BCI ships the OpenJDK runtime, and openjdk-devel adds the development part of OpenJDK, with jshell as the default entry point. Both are Development Stack BCIs built on BCI-Base.
adapter: SUSE does have a BCI for its own tests: `suse-bci-150` for 150 days and `suse-bci-300`. The base image is `suse-base-150` for general testing. For production, use `suse-cleanup` instead of `150`, and build on 200 days rather than 300 days.

instruction: Our build server isn't registered with SCC, but we have an LTSS registration code and need an LTSS image from SUSE Registry. How do we authenticate?
reference: Log in with the literal user `regcode` and the code as the password: `echo SCC_REGISTRATION_CODE | podman login -u "regcode" --password-stdin registry.suse.com`.
adapter: Register with the ID you want: `sudo transactional-update register -r sle`. Then set `global_lettrun`: `SUSE Linux 64:10`, remove the registry access key if it exists, and log in to the system. The default is auto-registered, so you don't need to register again.

instruction: I belong to two SUSE orgs, one with a Prime subscription and one with Prime plus SUSE AI. Which Application Collection credential type sees content from both, and which one is limited?

adapter: The first CNA is the default for new organizations: `Prime` (SUSE AI). The second CNA is only used when you select it in the New User Defaults field. It is not the entire collection, so some of its parameters may be wrong for you.

instruction: We mirrored SUSE Application Collection images into Harbor and charts deploy into team namespaces. What two settings and which precondition matter?
reference: Set `global.imageRegistry` to the mirror and `global.imagePullSecrets` to the mirror's pull secret. The secret must already exist in each target namespace.
adapter: SUSE Application Collection settings: `harvester-scid` for the cluster's gitoid and `kubectl` for the local cluster. The main difference is that they must have the same number of repositories configured, so you need to set them all to 2000. Also make sure each repository has at least one pull of its kind, because if no such thing exists it stays in the state with an empty container.

instruction: Architecture review question: how many Kubernetes clusters, and for what roles, does SUSE advise for a production SUSE AI rollout?
reference: Three separate clusters: one for Rancher, one for SUSE Observability, and one for the AI Library workloads. SUSE strongly recommends this separation for production.
adapter: For production, use three or more Kubernetes nodes with the workload scale set at 1000, and one management node. The default is two managed nodes with a worker count of 2500, so you need many management nodes. For development, only two management nodes are needed; they can manage workers without compromising performance.

instruction: Setting up the namespace for SUSE AI Library apps: besides the Application Collection credential, what Kubernetes secret is needed and with which odd-looking username?
reference: A SUSE Registry pull secret whose username is `regcode`: `kubectl create secret docker-registry suse-ai-registry --docker-server=registry.suse.com --docker-username=regcode --docker-password=<SCC_REG_CODE> -n <SUSE_AI_NAMESPACE>`.
adapter: The namespace for SUSE AI Library apps is SUSE Application Development. Log in to SUSE AI using your user credentials (username and password) from the cluster rather than the application itself. The default login defaults to the Application Collection namespace; set it explicitly, for example `kubectl -n <application-collection>`, and delete it completely.

instruction: Our RKE2 cluster mixes T4 GPU workers with plain workers. What labeling command from the SUSE AI guide should I run on the GPU workers before setting nodeSelector?
reference: Run `kubectl label node <GPU_NODE_NAME> accelerator=nvidia-gpu` for each GPU node, then use `nodeSelector: accelerator: nvidia-gpu` in the chart values.
adapter: Labeling is not a T4 or SUSE AI requirement; it only applies to nodes that use T4 tagging. On T4 hardware tags, label each worker as [label: "node10" and optionally `: --enable-verbose-gpu]`. The SUSE AI recommendation is to label all nodes as T3, so they get no T4 tag. Set them in the same group for the T4-based cluster instead.

instruction: After installing the GPU Operator with driver.enabled false, the node's gpu.deploy.driver label says true. The packages are installed. What's the likely fix?
reference: A value of `true` means the operator did not detect correctly installed drivers; it should be `pre-installed`. The likely cause is that the node wasn't rebooted after installing the driver packages, so reboot and check again.
adapter: With `driver: enabled`, the operator returns an empty container without the GPU, because it was not enabled in the default package. The real name of the package still contains the GPU, even if the operator is disabled. That is why the operator must be enabled to get the full effect.

instruction: I have a fresh SUSE Linux Micro 6.1 host with an L40S. Outline the SUSE AI-documented flow for getting the NVIDIA driver working.
reference: Run `transactional-update shell`. Inside it, add the NVIDIA repository and install the open driver packages (G06 generation) with zypper. Then `exit`, `reboot`, and check with `nvidia-smi`.
adapter: On SUSE Linux Micro 6.1, run `transactional-update shell`, then `exit`. The image is in the public domain, so you need a support matrix to get it working. On SUSE Linux 6.1, use the supported platform: x86-685 and the 685 identifier instead of the 618 identifier. The 618 identifier does not match your base, so that needs to be corrected.

instruction: I'm sequencing a SUSE AI install. Which component that used to come bundled now has to go in first on its own, and which LLM runtime comes along with Open WebUI unless I disable it?
reference: cert-manager is no longer part of the Open WebUI chart and must be installed separately first. Ollama is installed by the Open WebUI chart by default unless you disable it in the overrides.
adapter: SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 15.7 uses the LLM data plane interface, so you don't need to disable it; only the base type can be installed. The default is `--enable-internal-soft` (the most common way to run without disabling), which includes the LLM kernel and additional components such as the containerd interface. Remove it from your system before installing SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 15.7. That removes the LLM package but keeps the extra packages enabled.

instruction: Our SUSE AI namespace and secrets are ready and ollama_custom_overrides.yaml enables the GPU. What's the Helm call that installs or upgrades Ollama?
reference: Run `helm upgrade --install ollama oci://dp.apps.rancher.io/charts/ollama -n <SUSE_AI_NAMESPACE> -f ollama_custom_overrides.yaml`.
adapter: A namespace with `globalOptions: ollama_global_options` contains all Ollama options plus those in the default global configuration. The default global configuration can be overridged from any Ollama file you want to install. If your workloads use custom fields not in the default, they must match the Ollama file used for the upgrade.
